event.title: PMA Films: The History of Concrete
event.description: Directed by John Wilson. 101 minutes (followed by pre-recorded discussion). Not Rated. In English. This screening will be followed by a pre-recorded, 15-minute discussion between director John Wilson and Josh Safdie. Following the finale of his acclaimed HBO series “How To with John Wilson”, NYC documentarian John Wilson looks to the bedrock of his beloved New York City for inspiration and structure. Concrete, the world’s most widely used building material, appears as an ever-present life force, and John sets out to make the definitive documentary on the matter. After attending a workshop on how to write and sell a Hallmark movie, he decides to use the industry-approved Hallmark formula to tell this seemingly drab story and increase his movie’s appeal. But his foundation soon begins to crumble—literally and figuratively—as he struggles to balance artistic freedom with the realities of the modern film industry.

event.title: PMA Films: Out at Six (Presented with Finding Our Voices)
event.description: Directed by Livi Kessel. 55 minutes (followed by Survivor-Speaks discussion). Not Rated. In Hebrew with English subtitles. This screening will be followed by a panel discussion with domestic abuse survivors, coordinated by Finding Our Voices. Finding Our Voices is the grassroots nonprofit breaking the silence of domestic abuse around Maine, including in schools, and providing practical resources and heart-healing support to women survivors and their children. Registration for this screening is recommended, and admission is pay-what-you-want. When teenage Livi is the first in her friend group to move in with a man, her girl friends are excited for her. But her world slowly gets smaller and more dangerous as he increasingly isolates and psychologically terrorizes her. The powerful documentary chronicles Livi’s journey against Prof. Jane Monkton Smith’s chilling and seminal timeline of the eight stages that precede intimate partner murder. Through Livi’s conversations with those who knew her while she was trapped in the domestic abuse, the film illuminates the dangerous gray zone of psychological abuse AKA coercive control that often hides in plain sight. Topics of the post-screening discussion will include how to best help someone you worry is trapped in an unhealthy intimate partner relationship, and the role the community can play in safeguarding our neighbors from dangerous family members. For more information about Finding Our Voices visit https://findingourvoices.net

event.title: A Bizarre Victorian Bazaar: An Exhibition of Oddities and the Obscure
event.description: Our outdoor event, A Bizarre Victorian Bazaar: An Exhibition of Oddities and the Obscure, will return the Victoria Mansion this fall! This one-day fair kicks off the Halloween season with an educational (and entertaining!) take on Victorian folklore, customs, Spiritualism, and more. Learn about poison books and wallpaper, how purported mediums conducted seances, and why some elite Victorians held mummy unwrapping parties. Have your cards or runes read, create Victorian crafts, and much, much more! This fair will have activities and games for kids throughout the day. Plus, a visit from “Dracula,” music by One-Eared Cat, and readings from “penny dreadfuls.” We’ll also have Sullivan House Bakery onsite for visitors who want to grab a bite to eat while they enjoy demonstrations and performances on the lawn. Exhibitors and performers include: Phillips Puppets Osher Map Library Portland Ballet Andrew Harris Saco Museum’s Cabinet of Curiosities …and more! This event is designed for visitors ages 8 and up. We encourage caregiver discretion for younger and more sensitive children. Keep an eye on our Events webpage, and our Facebook and Instagram pages in the coming weeks as we announce more. A full schedule of events will be available onsite on the day of the event, and a preliminary schedule of events will be available closer to the event date. event.title: PMA Films: “A Few Small Odysseys”: Good Time (2017)
event.description: Directed by Josh Safdie and Benny Safdie. 101 minutes. Rated R. In English. Following the mind-bending Heaven Knows What, celebrated filmmakers Josh and Benny Safdie return to the mean streets of New York City with Good Time, a hypnotic crime thriller that explores with bracing immediacy the tragic sway of family and fate. After a botched bank robbery lands his younger brother in prison, Constantine “Connie” Nikas (Robert Pattinson) embarks on a twisted odyssey through the city’s underworld in an increasingly desperate—and dangerous—attempt to get his brother Nick (Benny Safdie) out of jail. Over the course of one adrenalized night, Connie finds himself on a mad descent into violence and mayhem as he races against the clock to save his brother and himself, knowing their lives hang in the balance.

event.title: PMA Films: Aanikoobijigan [ancestor / great-grandparent / great-grandchild] (Free Screening)
event.description: Directed by Adam Khalil and Zack Khalil. 80 minutes. Not Rated. In English and Anishinaabemowin with English subtitles. Aanikoobijigan [ancestor / great-grandparent / great-grandchild] documents the emotional and vital work of MACPRA (Michigan Anishinaabek Cultural Preservation and Repatriation Alliance). This alliance, made up of repatriation specialists representing all Michigan tribes, fights to bring their Ancestors and funerary objects home from settler colonial institutions like museums, libraries, and archives. Adam and Zack Khalil’s monumental and formally daring film follows the pressing struggle to rebury Indigenous human remains that have been held in sterile storage, laying bare the history of Indigenous collections and the battle to recognize and enforce the laws intended to facilitate their repatriation to the communities they were originally stolen from. Using an essayistic approach alongside vérité portraits, the film celebrates the courageous individuals who carry out this hard and emotionally draining labor of return. — Sundance Film Festival

event.title: PMA Films: The Work in Progress (with filmmaker Ian Cheney)
event.description: Directed by Ian Cheney. 100 minutes (followed by discussion). Not Rated. In English. This screening will be followed by a discussion with director Ian Cheney. If you were invited to sit at a table with someone you’ve never met before and answer handwritten questions from a wooden box about the state of America, would you run the other way? The Work in Progress invites strangers from across generations and geographies to engage in candid discussions about America’s ever-evolving democracy, identity, and definitions of community — and where the heck we go from here. Guided by questions posed by Executive Producer Robert Reich, participants sit down in a series of conversations with one another to explore the country they’re living in now and the one they still believe is possible. These encounters are intercut with portraits of Americans at work — in woodshops, laboratories, fields, board rooms, recording studios, theaters, and beyond. The message is simple but profound: America can work because, in many ways, it’s already working. And a central part of the work ahead is to reclaim the practices of dialogue, debate, compromise, and perhaps most importantly, listening, so that we might find our footing again. What emerges in The Work in Progress is an unusual and provocative glimpse of America in its 250th year, and an invitation to all Americans to pull up a chair, invite a stranger, and lend an ear.

event.title: Artists in Conversation featuring Elizabeth Atterbury, Sascha Braunig, and Eve Biddle
event.description: Free. Registration requested. Open to PMA members and the public, including students from local BFA and MFA programs. The PMA brings together three artists of the same generation — Elizabeth Atterbury, Eve Biddle, and Sascha Braunig — for a rare conversation timed to a brief overlap of Biddle and Braunig’s exhibitions. Though their practices span different media and perspectives, Atterbury, Biddle, and Braunig share intersecting concerns and generational context. Join them in conversation for an evening exploring where their work converges, diverges, and surprises. About Artists in Conversation About Artists in Conversation Artists in Conversation is a program series at the Portland Museum of Art that brings artists together for public dialogue around shared moments of exhibition, generation, or theme. Launched in November 2026, the series creates opportunities for intergenerational dialogue and interdisciplinary exchange, pairing emerging and established artists in conversations that reveal unexpected connections across practice and perspective. Open to PMA members and the public, Artists in Conversation invites audiences into the ideas and relationships shaping contemporary art today. Artists in Conversation is made possible with the generous support of Bruce Moore and Michael Alper. Exhibitions Eve Biddle: Wonderlands on view now through January 24, 2027 Sascha Braunig: Wrist Painter on view Nov 13, 2026 through March 14, 2027 Elizabeth Atterbury (b.1982) is an artist based in Portland, Maine. Her studio practice moves between two and three dimensions and is grounded by a curiosity in language and objects/object-making. Often of personal significance, the forms used in her work draw from multiple sources including memories, family history, the natural world, and everyday life. Solo exhibitions include, The Center for Maine Contemporary Art, Rockland, ME, The Clark Art Institute, Williamstown, MA, Colby College Museum of Art, Waterville, ME, DOCUMENT, Chicago, IL and Lisbon, Portugal, and Mrs. Maspeth, NY. Group exhibitions include The Farnsworth Art Museum, Rockland, ME, deCordova Sculpture Park and Museum, Lincoln, MA, Portland Museum of Art, Portland, ME, Crisp-Ellert Art Museum, St.Augustine, FL, and The ICA at MECA&D, Portland, ME, among others. Atterbury’s work is in the collection of the Portland Museum of Art, The Farnsworth Art Museum, the Colby College Museum of Art and CELINE. Since 2017, Elizabeth Atterbury and artist Anna Hepler have collaborated on four Percent for Art commissions across the state of Maine. Eve Biddle (born 1982) is an artist, culture maker, and collaborator. Her work lies at the intersection of making objects, making connections between people, curating, building projects and institutions, helping to bring other artists’ art into the world, and making and facilitating public art. Her creative process is deeply personal, shaped by familial influences including her parents’ photography and sculpture, and her own bodily experiences—both beautiful and peculiar. She’s a founding co-director of the Wassaic Project, a contemporary art institution in Wassaic, NY. Recent exhibitions include The Portland Museum of Art, Portland, ME, The Williams College Museum of Art in Williamstown, MA, Davidson Gallery in New York City, The Buffalo Institute for Contemporary Art in Buffalo, NY, The Museum of Art and Design, New York City and Sargent’s Daughters, New York City. Sascha Braunig (b. 1983, Qualicum Beach, BC) devotes her critical focus to the capaciousness and limitations of the feminine form under duress. Braunig’s figures teeter towards overextension—waists are pinched to extremity; appendages are restricted or decked in barbs; phantom silhouettes sinuously negotiate and adapt to the contours of their technicolor environments. Drawing on feminist artistic discourse, Braunig’s imaginaries engage the ways that gender performance and systems of power are replicated. Training, fitting, and reinforcement are recurring motifs in the severe and sometimes sinister crucibles which Braunig’s figures endure. Cast in vibrant complementary palettes and anchored through Braunig’s graphic, tensile formal vocabulary, her images recapitulate and usurp foundational codes of gendered visuality to create surreal and unequivocally emblematic scenes. Sascha Braunig holds a BFA from Cooper Union and an MFA in painting from Yale University, and has been awarded residencies at MacDowell, the Sharpe-Walentas Studio Program, and Surf Point. Selected solo exhibitions include François Ghebaly, New York and Los Angeles, USA; Oakville Galleries, Ontario, Canada; Magenta Plains, New York, USA; Office Baroque, Brussels, Belgium; Kunstall Stavanger, Norway; Atlanta Contemporary, Atlanta, USA; and MoMA PS1, New York, USA. Her work has been featured in institutional exhibitions including the Quebec City Biennial; Oakville Galleries, Ontario, Canada; the Portland Museum of Art, Portland, USA; National Gallery of Victoria, Melbourne, Australia; Aïshti Foundation, Beirut, Lebanon; Museum of Contemporary Art Cleveland, Cleveland, USA; and the New Museum Triennial, New York, USA.
